text: Julien Simon Oct 25, 2026 1 Share macOS 27 put a language model on every Mac that can run Apple Intelligence, and any script can call it: type fm respond in a terminal and it answers.[1] So what is it? How is it built, who built it, and what is it good for? Apple's answers fit in three sentences. The model is Core Advanced, the larger of Apple's two on-device models, with 20 billion parameters of which 1 to 4 billion work at a time. Apple says it is "custom-built in collaboration with Google." It powers Siri's new voices and dictation, and the apps that call it.[2] Everything else you have to work out. I can't read Apple's weights. Apple's license bars decompiling, disassembling and reverse engineering its software, and I won't test that line: I opened no model file, decompiled or disassembled nothing, dumped no memory, attached no debugger and left the Mac's system protection on.[3] I watched the Mac from the outside instead, with tools macOS ships (a file-read trace that gives file names, positions and sizes but never contents, the system log, the memory and power counters, the lists of names Apple's frameworks export) and with Apple's public commands: what the model reads from disk, how much memory it holds, how much power it draws, how it counts text and how it answers. I did that on a MacBook Pro with an M3 Max and 48 GB, beside open models that run on the same Mac. Where Apple gives no reason for a choice, I give mine and label it "Assumption." The scripts and the data are in a public repository, where each finding is a numbered item with its hypothesis or question, experiment, results and conclusion.[4] Apple made a 20-billion-parameter model cost a Mac about what a 4-billion-parameter one does. It keeps the model in flash storage, wakes a few experts for each prompt, and runs them on the Neural Engine. Two seconds after a long request, Apple's model and its safety models held 2.0 GiB of memory; an open model of the same class, built the usual way, held about 15 GiB.[5] On the same 20 math problems, it used about a third of the energy of the best open build I ran.[6] You pay in math, where it finished last of four, and in control: you can't pin it or tune it.[7] And the one part of Google you can measure from outside is the tokenizer.[8] A model card is the page a lab publishes to say what a model is. Apple has not published one for Core Advanced, so here is the one I could build from outside. Each line says where it comes from: Apple's own words, my measurements on this Mac, my inferences from them, or third parties. The repository holds each line's data.[9] How Apple's on-device model runs on a Mac An app never touches the model. It calls Apple's Swift framework, the fm command or fm serve ; a system service, modelmanagerd , then opens sessions with two processes that run as a system user.[10] The safety process holds two 300-million-parameter models, a safety classifier and a guard for images, with their own, smaller tokenizer; by their names, they screen the request. The log also names a text sanitizer, a deny-list of output tokens and an output safety configuration. The main process runs Core Advanced: a tokenizer, a small adapter for the use case, an image encoder, the dense block that picks experts, the experts, and a small draft model, which by its name guesses a few tokens ahead for the main model to check. 636 MiB of model pages stay loaded on the Neural Engine; the rest stays in a 4.95 GB file in flash, and a cache brings in the experts a prompt picks.[10] A request the device cannot handle goes to Private Cloud Compute, Apple's server models, and an app must choose that model itself.[11] Two things stand out. First, Apple dropped adapters for developers in OS 27 but kept them for itself: the bundle the public API loads is the base model plus an adapter named for it, and Apple's catalog lists a draft model for 135 use cases.[10] Assumption: Apple tunes each of its own features with a small adapter it ships and retrains with each OS, and a third-party adapter, trained on last year's base model, would break at every update. Second, the safety models are a separate process with a separate tokenizer. Apple can update them without touching the main model, and they cost memory, 0.7 GiB of the 2.0. Apple names the jobs. On its research page, Core Advanced is "natively multimodal, enabling helpful features like expressive voices and higher-accuracy dictation," and Siri's new voices are "powered by" it.[2] For apps, Apple's developer guide lists what the on-device model is for: summarizing, extracting entities, understanding, refining and classifying text, creative writing, tags and game dialog. The same guide lists three "capabilities to avoid": basic math, code and logical reasoning. Apple's 2025 report said its earlier on-device model "is not designed to be a chatbot for general world knowledge."[12] Then Apple names the limit. "Traditional large language models," its page says, "require all weights to reside in active memory (DRAM), creating a massive footprint that limits scalability on consumer hardware."[13] A Mac's memory is shared by the CPU, the GPU and every app you have open. The model sits in it all day, beside your browser and your editor, and on a laptop it runs on a battery. Apple's storage page sets its larger tier for Macs with an M3 or later and at least 12 GB, and MacRumors says that is what Core Advanced requires.[14] So the job is a model good enough for dozens of short tasks, light enough in memory to stay loaded next to your apps, and frugal enough with power to run voice and dictation all day. Three of the choices below are new this year: experts kept in flash, experts chosen per prompt, and a model that runs at more than one size. Apple made the other four before: the Neural Engine, heavy compression, separate safety models and a short task list.[15] A mixture-of-experts model splits each layer into many small networks, the experts, and runs only a few for each token. The usual design picks new experts for every token, so every expert must sit in memory. Apple's page says why that does not work here: "NAND-to-DRAM bandwidth is too slow to swap weights token by token, as standard MoE models require." So Core Advanced "makes routing decisions per prompt." A small dense block picks a fixed set of experts when it reads your prompt and reselects them from time to time as it writes, with "a high percentage of always-active 'shared experts'" to keep the traffic down.[13] This is Apple's own line of research. In December 2023, Apple researchers showed how to run models "that exceed the available DRAM capacity by storing the model parameters in flash memory," and warned that flash is fast for large reads, not for "smaller, random reads."[16] In January 2025 they described Instruction-Following Pruning, which fixes the parameters for a task once and so "significantly reduces the weight loading cost."[17] Apple says Core Advanced is built on it.[13] And on October 5th, 2026, six Apple researchers posted a paper on routing for models on devices, where the workload "becomes an I/O-bound one," with experts "reloaded every S inference steps."[18] The Mac shows the design at work. While the model answers, it reads one 4.95 GB file in blocks of exactly 294,912 bytes. On the first prompts after loading, it reads about 1% of the file a fifth of a second in; later prompts, with experts already in memory, read less. Then it reads a few blocks at a steady rhythm: every 32 tokens in a code answer written at 58 tokens a second, every 32 in an essay at 33 tokens a second, every 31 in a geology answer at 45.[19] The rhythm is counted in tokens, not seconds. Assumption: the model reselects every 32 tokens; on a long prompt the gaps were irregular, which fits reselections that find their experts already in memory and read nothing.[19] Assumption: the blocks are experts; the file name, Apple's description and the byte count all point there, and other shapes give the same count.[20] Now compare an open model of the same class, built for per-token routing. Google's Gemma 4 26B A4B stores 25.2 billion parameters and runs 3.8 billion for each token, 8 of its 128 experts plus a shared one.[21] At 4 bits on the same Mac, two seconds after the same long request, its server held about 15 GiB. Apple's two processes held 2.0 GiB.[5] That is the case for Apple's design in one comparison: the same idea, a big model with a small part at work, costs seven times the memory when experts change at every token. About half of that is bit width, 4 bits against about 2; the rest is that per-token routing makes the server hold every expert. Google aims that model at "consumer GPUs and workstations," not phones.[21] Google's answer for small devices is different again. Gemma 3n keeps large per-layer embedding tables out of accelerator memory, so only "the core transformer weights" must sit there, and its larger model contains the smaller one; the small Gemma 4 models carry the same per-layer embeddings.[22] Assumption: Google builds for many makers' phones and boards, so it splits the model by kind of parameter, which any device can do; Apple builds for one family of chips and one storage system it controls, so it splits the model by expert and leans on fast flash. (My Gemma memory figures do not show Google's design at work: by my reading of its 8.1 GiB, the server kept all of Gemma 4 E4B's 8 billion parameters in memory.[22]) Apple also lets the model run at more than one size. Core Advanced "uses a predetermined number of active parameters tailored to each specific use case," from 1 to 4 billion, so weights are "loaded incrementally across requests of varying difficulty."[13] Apple's only published results for Core Advanced, for voice and dictation, were measured "At its 1-billion-parameter activation size."[23] Assumption: speech, which runs all the time, uses the smallest size, and text tasks use more. Google described a similar switch for Gemma 3n and says it is "not part of today’s launched implementations."[22] Assumption, on the 32-token period: Apple's October paper found that "a segment length of 16 outperforms a segment length of 32" on every benchmark it ran, so Apple ships 32 to halve the flash reads and accepts a small loss in quality.[18] Apple's 2025 report says "we compressed the on-device model to 2 bits-per-weight," and its new page says the new models were compressed with the same kind of training, without a bit width.[24] What the Mac shows fits 2 bits. The Neural Engine's log counts 636 MiB of model pages that stay loaded, at most 2.7 billion weights at 2 bits, which fits 1 to 4 billion active. One 294,912-byte block is exactly the size of one expert of the dimensions in Apple's October paper at 2 bits.[25] Assumption: the bit width serves the flash design too, because every bit saved is a byte not read at each reselection. Apple's 2024 report already described its on-device model "running on Apple Neural Engine."[26] On this Mac, the Neural Engine drew 4.2 watts while the model read a long prompt and 3.8 while it wrote, and the GPU stayed at its idle clock.[27] Apple gives no reason specific to the chip; its 2025 report credits its optimizations as a whole with "reducing power consumption."[24] I measured what that buys. The same 20 grade-school math problems went to Apple's model and to three open models on the GPU, Google's Gemma 3 4B and Gemma 4 E4B and Alibaba's Qwen3 4B, while macOS's power meter sampled the chip twice a second. Apple's model used about a third of the energy of the best open build for the same 20 problems, and the least per problem solved, though it solved only 13 of them.[6] Halving the open builds' weights from 8 bits to 4 did not lower their energy by more than the run-to-run noise. The open builds run about 4 billion parameters per token, close to Apple's 1 to 4 billion, and Apple's answers were a little shorter. Assumption: most of the gap is the Neural Engine.[6] Assumption: the Neural Engine is also why Apple routes per prompt. The Neural Engine runs programs compiled ahead of time, and the model's programs on this Mac are compiled for its chip family;[10] a set of experts that holds for 32 tokens suits it; a set that changes at every token would not. The flash design and the chip choice fit each other, and the GPU stays free for your apps. Apple says it uses "language-specific guardrail models," and that "Guardrails are a safety system tied to a specific model."[29] They run in their own process (see the diagram) and refused 4 of my 300 benchmark questions, one of them a grade-school problem about a race with Japanese and Chinese runners; the maintainers of an open-source tool saw them refuse the Apollo 11 plaque.[29] Apple gives no reason for a separate model. Assumption: a separate model can be swapped per language and updated without retraining the main one, and it puts the same check in front of every app. Apple chose control and paid for it in memory. The public API reports an 8,192-token window on this Mac, twice the 4,096 that Apple's documentation still states.[30] Assumption: the window is small because the memory budget is small; the attention cache alone takes 560 MiB at 8,192 tokens, and the wait for the first word grows with the square of the prompt, to 9.5 seconds at 6,900 tokens.[25][28] It matches Apple's task list: short inputs, short outputs. Apple and Google said in January that Apple's next models "will be based on Google's Gemini models and cloud technology." Apple's page says "custom-built in collaboration with Google," and that "we significantly scaled pre-training on the latest generation of cloud TPU accelerators," Google's chips, which Apple also used in 2024.[31] At a press briefing on June 8th, as 9to5Mac transcribed it, Apple's vice president of AI said the models were "refined using outputs from Gemini frontier models," and Craig Federighi said Apple uses "none of the models that Google deploys to their customers."[32] None of them names the tokenizer, the part of a model that cuts text into tokens, and a Mac can check it. Apple's fm count-tokens gave Gemma 3's count on all 429 strings I tried, from code to sentences in 18 languages; tokenizers from other labs matched on less than half. Google's own counting endpoint returned Apple's count on every string I sent it.[8] Apple adapted it: 775 of the 6,242 placeholder slots in Gemma's vocabulary no longer count as one token. Assumption: those are Apple's own control markers.[33] Why Gemini's tokenizer? Apple doesn't say. Assumption: Apple trains its small models on a larger teacher's predictions, as its 2024 and 2025 reports describe, and that kind of training needs the teacher's vocabulary; with Gemini as the teacher, the student takes Gemini's tokenizer. The Information reported in March, as two outlets relayed it, that Apple has the access to do that with Gemini; that is reported, not confirmed.[34] The published line of research is Apple's. Experts kept in flash and chosen per prompt run through Apple's papers from 2023 to this month and appear in none of Google's Gemma model cards.[16][17][18][22] The strongest case against that reading is in Apple's own October paper: a model pruned this way "cannot be pre-trained rather only upcycled," so it starts from a dense model someone trained first.[18] Assumption: that dense model was trained with Google's help, on Google's chips, with Gemini's tokenizer and Gemini as the teacher, and Apple then pruned it into its own design. That reading fits both "based on" and "collaboration". In March, I wrote that Apple had "opted out of the intelligence race entirely." That sentence needs an update, and it was partly right. The training leans on Google: its chips, its tokenizer and, by Apple's account, Gemini's outputs. The engineering and the hardware integration are Apple's: the flash design, the Neural Engine programs, the runtime around the model. For a company that sells devices, not models, it is a sensible split. And in June, Apple extended Private Cloud Compute to NVIDIA GPUs in Google Cloud, which updates my March note on where its Gemini-based model runs.[11] Math, first. On 100 grade-school problems, Apple's model solved 78 and the three open builds 89 to 94, a gap too large for chance; on 200 knowledge questions it sat in the middle.[7] That is what 1 to 4 billion active parameters at about 2 bits buys, and Apple says as much: basic math is on its list of things to avoid.[12] Then control. You can't pin the model: an Apple engineer wrote that there is "currently no pinning or model version retrieval API," and the model changes with the OS.[35] In one developer's test, the model's verdicts changed on 11 of 227 messages across the update, with the same code and prompt.[36] And you can't tune it: Apple dropped developer adapters in OS 27 "for performance reasons," an Apple staff member wrote.[37] Assumption: both follow from one choice, one base model per OS, replaced at every update, with Apple's own adapters retrained alongside it. So run your own test. Write 100 questions from your own work, run them through Apple's model and an open one with the same prompts at temperature 0, and count the questions only one of them gets right. If they disagree on 20, the winner needs 15 before the gap is more than chance.[7] Run it again after every OS update. Core Advanced is first-rate AI engineering. Apple took a 20-billion-parameter model, kept it in flash and made it run in about 2 GiB of a laptop's memory, on about a third of the energy of the open models I set beside it, with the GPU idle.[5][6][27] It did that with a design from its own research, from its 2023 flash paper to this month's routing paper, compiled for its own chip and wrapped in an operating-system service with its own safety models. No open model I ran works this way. Google's part is in the training: the chips, the tokenizer and, by Apple's account at a briefing 9to5Mac transcribed, outputs from Gemini models. The engineering that makes it fit on a Mac is Apple's. Use it for short, fixed-shape jobs where memory and battery matter more than reasoning: summaries, extraction, classification, tags, rewrites. Do not use it for math, code or anything that needs a pinned version or a tuned model; run an open model for those. Next, Apple owes a technical report, announced for the summer and still missing as of October 25th.[38] Assumption: the next model moves to Gemma 4's tokenizer, which Google's own software already assigns to its newest Gemini models, and Apple ships the variable sizes of its October paper so that an app can trade speed for quality.[39] And Apple should release the weights. They already sit on every eligible Mac, 4.95 GB of them, and Apple has published open weights before, on Hugging Face: OpenELM under a research-only license, DCLM-7B under its sample-code license.[40] Open weights under a license that allows commercial use would let developers pin a version, tune the model for their own jobs, and check for themselves what came from Google. Today the license bars taking it apart. Apple built something new and very good here; it should let people study it and build on it. [1] Author's observation, October 24th, 2026, on the MacBook Pro in note [4]; the tool is /usr/bin/fm . fm --help prints the title "Apple Foundation Models CLI", the commands available , chat , count-tokens , license , respond , schema and serve , and the model system , "On-device Apple Foundation Model (default)" (saved in the repository as data/fm_help.txt ). Apple's WWDC26 session 334 calls it "the brand new fm command introduced in macOS 27". Apple's storage page for Apple Intelligence , published October 22nd, 2026, says the next generation of Apple Intelligence "is automatically available on eligible devices as part of the operating system when you update to the 27.0 software releases", and adds "in supported languages and regions". [2] Apple Machine Learning Research, "Introducing the Third Generation of Apple's Foundation Models" , June 8th, 2026 (updated September 9th, 2026), accessed October 24th, 2026: "At the heart of this architecture is our third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), a family of five foundation models custom-built in collaboration with Google."; "AFM 3 Core Advanced is unlocked by and optimized for our most capable Apple silicon systems"; a "20-billion-parameter model" that "uses a sparse architecture, activating just 1 to 4 billion parameters at a time depending on the request"; it is "natively multimodal, enabling helpful features like expressive voices and higher-accuracy dictation." Under related reading: "Siri Expressive Voices synthesize rich, configurable speech in real time and entirely on device, powered by AFM 3 Core Advanced, Apple’s most powerful on-device foundation model." The page does not name Gemini. Apple's public API reports Core Advanced on the Mac in note [4] (repository item 12). Apple's own researchers describe the model the same way: the voice paper Memory Efficient Audio Synthesis with Decoupled Temporal Depth Diffusion Transformers , arXiv 2607.23811v2, August 17th, 2026, eleven authors, affiliation Apple, says "AFM 3 Core Advanced is natively multimodal and built on a sparse, 20-billion-parameter architecture that uses Instruction-Following Pruning (IFP) Hou et al. (2025)", with "1–4 billion active parameters, reselected periodically during generation" and "a set of always-active shared experts". [3] Apple, Software License Agreement for macOS, the copy installed on the Mac in note [4] at /Library/Documentation/License.lpdf/Contents/Resources/English.lproj/License.html (read October 25th, 2026; saved by hand), section N, "No Reverse Engineering": "You may not, and you agree not to or enable others to, copy (except as expressly permitted by this License or by the Usage Rules if they are applicable to you), decompile, reverse engineer, disassemble, attempt to derive the source code or training data of, decrypt, modify, or create derivative works of the Apple Software or any services provided by the Apple Software or any part thereof (except as and only to the extent any foregoing restriction is prohibited by applicable law or by licensing terms governing use of Open-Sourced Components that may be included with the Apple Software)." The fm tool's own notice, printed by fm license --show on October 24th, 2026, binds the user to that license and adds, in capitals, "YOU ARE ALSO AGREEING TO NOT PROGRAMMATICALLY ACCESS OR USE APPLE MODELS THROUGH APPLE SOFTWARE OR SERVICES EXCEPT AS EXPRESSLY PERMITTED". Apple's WWDC26 session 241 says "I can even plug fm into shell scripts to summarize documents, extract information, or generate content"; I ran fm and fm serve from scripts on my own Mac. When a developer asked on Apple's forums whether an app distributed to users may call fm serve , the Apple Designer's reply pointed to the Developer Program License Agreement and gave no yes or no. [4] Author's measurements, October 24th and 25th, 2026, on a MacBook Pro (Apple M3 Max, 48 GB, macOS 27.0.1, build 26A434). Companion repository, apple-fm-mac : one folder per finding, findings/01-model-card/ to findings/16-attention-cache-shape/ , numbered by topic; "item 05" in these notes means findings/05-power-and-energy/ . Each item gives the hypothesis (or the question, when none was written first), the experiment with its commands and files, the results, and the conclusion with what it does not show; scripts/check_numbers.py recomputes the numbers from the data files, except the expert-read cadence, which is worked in item 02. Code is under the MIT license; text and data under CC BY 4.0. Method boundary: the tools were fs_usage (system-call names, file descriptors, offsets and sizes, never contents), footprint and vmmap (memory counters and region layout), powermetrics (power counters), the unified log, Apple's public fm tool and Foundation Models API, and the names that Apple's frameworks export ( dyld_info -exports , names only). No model file was opened, nothing was decompiled or disassembled, no process memory was dumped or sampled, no debugger was attached, and System Integrity Protection stayed on. The raw file-read traces, memory maps and name listings are not in the repository, because they name files in Apple's protected asset folder; the numbers they gave are. Hypotheses written before their tests: H1, Gemma 3 within 10 points of Apple's model on both tests (failed, math gap 11 points; item 09); H2, Apple's model about as good as Gemma 3 on events from September 2024 on, within 20 points (held; item 13); H3, Apple's model below every open build in energy per solved problem (held; item 05); H4, the per-token open model holds 12 GiB or more two seconds after the request (held; item 04); H5, the long-context reselection period between 28 and 36 tokens (neither held nor failed; item 02). [5] Repository item 04 . Memory by macOS's footprint tool, for each process its whole footprint plus the Neural Engine memory that macOS leaves out of it, read at the same three moments of one 5,000-token request: idle (one second after a one-word request), during (Apple: one snapshot three seconds into the prefill; open builds: the largest of 39 to 113 readings during the request) and after (two seconds after the request ended). Apple, after: main process 293 MiB plus 1,068 MiB of Neural Engine memory, 1,361 MiB; second process, which runs the safety models, 140 plus 535 MiB, 675 MiB. Author's calculation: 1,361 + 675 = 2,036. The result is in MiB, about 2.0 GiB. Author's calculation: 675 ÷ 2,036 ≈ 0.33. That is the safety process's share. Apple at idle: 2,848 MiB; during: 3,437 MiB, both processes, so between 2.0 and 3.4 GiB at every moment measured. Dense open builds, each mlx_lm.server process, after: 3.4 to 4.6 GiB at 4 bits and 5.6 to 8.1 GiB at 8 bits. Gemma 4 26B A4B at 4 bits, October 25th, 2026: idle 14.0 GiB, during 16.0, after 15.0, ten seconds later 15.0; footprint prints whole gigabytes at that size, so these figures are good to about 1 GiB. Its hypothesis was written before the run ( data/compare/HYPOTHESIS_moe_footprint.md ). Not measured: Apple's memory after minutes of rest, and any Mac with less memory. Author's calculation: 15.0 ÷ 1.99 ≈ 7.5. That is the ratio behind "seven times"; with footprint 's 1 GiB steps it lies between 7 and 8. The open build ran at 4 bits and Apple's weights are about 2 bits per weight (note [25]), so about half of the ratio is bit width. footprint does not count the operating system's file cache of the 4.95 GB expert file, which macOS can evict. [6] Repository item 05 . powermetrics (CPU, GPU and Neural Engine power, every 500 ms, run as root) while each model answered the same 20 GSM8K test problems through the same client code (Apple's model through fm serve , the open builds through mlx_lm.server ), with an idle baseline subtracted. The scripts' totals were recomputed from the raw samples by a second script with its own parser ( scripts/energy_recheck.py ), within 0.5 J. 8-bit set, October 25th, 2026, 00:48: Apple 464.6 J (13 of 20 solved, the 14th refused by the guardrail), 23.2 J a problem, 35.7 J per problem solved; Qwen3 4B 1,272.9 J (20 solved, 63.6 J); Gemma 3 4B 1,595.3 J (19 solved, 84.0 J per solved problem); Gemma 4 E4B 1,941.7 J (19 solved, 102.2 J). Author's calculation: 464.6 ÷ 1,272.9 ≈ 0.365. That is Apple's total as a share of the best open build's. 4-bit set, clean run, 07:50: Apple 529.7 J (40.7 per solved problem), Qwen3 1,529.9 J (76.5), Gemma 4 E4B 1,680.3 J (88.4), Gemma 3 1,716.4 J (95.4). Author's calculation: 529.7 ÷ 1,529.9 ≈ 0.346. A first 4-bit run, at 01:33, is not used: the Mac slept twice during it, and after it woke the GPU ran at about 1,040 MHz instead of 1,380, which roughly halved the energy of two open builds (Qwen3 858.9 J against 1,529.9). Author's calculation: 1,529.9 ÷ 858.9 ≈ 1.78. All three runs were on battery. Limits: no DRAM or SSD power, which powermetrics does not report on this Mac; 20 problems; one run per set; answer lengths not recorded. Run-to-run noise: Apple's own total moved from 464.6 J to 529.7 J between the two sets, and the idle baselines were 185 and 461 mW; against that, Qwen3 rose from 1,272.9 J at 8 bits to 1,529.9 J at 4 bits and Gemma 4 E4B fell from 1,941.7 J to 1,680.3 J. Answer lengths, from the 100 math problems of repository item 09 (same prompts): Apple wrote 24,845 tokens, Qwen3 27,265 and Gemma 4 34,015, so part of the gap is shorter answers. SSD power, which Apple's flash reads use, is not counted. [7] Repository item 09. 100 problems from the GSM8K test split and 200 questions from the MMLU test split, drawn with seed 7, zero-shot, temperature 0, the same prompts and scoring for every model. Apple's model ran through fm serve with no output cap; the open models ran as 8-bit MLX builds ( Gemma 3 4B , Gemma 4 E4B , Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 ) with thinking off, which favors Apple's model, since it has none. Math: Apple 78, Gemma 3 89, Gemma 4 94, Qwen3 93. Knowledge: Apple 134 (67.0%), Gemma 3 118 (59.0%), Gemma 4 139 (69.5%), Qwen3 144 (72.0%). Questions only one model of the pair got right, with the exact two-sided McNemar p: math 13 to 2 (p = 0.007), 18 to 2 (p = 0.0004), 17 to 2 (p = 0.0007); knowledge, open model against Apple, 14 to 30 (p = 0.023; 0.068 after Holm's correction for three comparisons), 23 to 18 (p = 0.53), 25 to 15 (p = 0.15). Rerun behind a local server with the client code used for Apple's model, no count moved by more than 1. Apple's guardrail refused 4 of the 300 requests, each counted wrong. fm serve adds about 46 framing tokens to every request that I could not read (item 08). Worked example for the advice: with 20 questions on which two models disagree, 15 to 5 gives p = 0.041 and 14 to 6 gives p = 0.115 (exact two-sided test, author's calculation). The open builds were capped at 1,000 tokens for math and 8 for knowledge, and Apple's model ran uncapped. Read from their final answers, the eight capped knowledge replies change Qwen3 to 150 of 200 (75.0%; 28 to 12 on the questions only one model got right, p = 0.017), still above Apple. [8] Repository item 07. Each of 429 strings was counted with Apple's fm count-tokens -q , which returns one token more than the text alone (subtracted), and with each public tokenizer through the Hugging Face tokenizers library (OpenAI's tiktoken for GPT-4 and GPT-4o). Gemma 3 ( unsloth/gemma-3-4b-it , whose tokenizer file has the same git object id as the one in Google's own repository): 429 of 429. Gemma 3n 429 of 429; Gemma 4 425 of 429 (it differs on four strings with an HTML heading tag); Gemma 2 75.5%; Mistral Nemo 44.5%, Qwen 2.5 42.0%, GPT-4o 36.1%, DeepSeek V3 33.3%, Llama 3.1 30.8%, GPT-4 30.3%, GPT-2 24.5%, Phi-3.5 mini 20.7%. Google's token-counting endpoint returned Apple's count on all 257 public strings sent to it, under each of four model names, gemma-4-31b-it and gemini-3.1-pro-preview among them. On four strings with an HTML heading tag, where Gemma 4's own tokenizer gives 13 or 14 tokens, the endpoint returned Apple's 7 or 8 under both names, so its count is not evidence for any one model's tokenizer. Google says Gemma 3 uses the tokenizer of Gemini 2.0 ( Gemma 3 Technical Report , section 2.2: "We use the same tokenizer as Gemini 2.0"). Equal counts show the same vocabulary in practice; they cannot show where the weights came from. The strings: English prose, code, sentences in 18 languages, numbers, URLs, emoji and rare words; 172 of them are private and the repository holds only their counts.
